Why I build things people actually use

Every weekend at Bean There Cafe I work the morning rush, and I have learned more about people from that counter than from any textbook. Regulars order the same drink for years. A nervous new customer needs one calm person to show them where the lids are. I try to be that person. Twelve hours a week behind the bar taught me that a process only works if the person running it can explain it to someone else in ten seconds.

Robotics taught me the same lesson on a bigger scale. As build lead for the Lakeview robotics team, I am responsible for the mechanical design our drive team uses in competition. Last season our intake jammed in almost every match. I spent three weekends with a tape measure and a cheap camera recording every failure, until the pattern was obvious: the intake jammed whenever the approach angle grew too steep. I learned to test before I trust a design, and to write down what I find so the next person does not have to rediscover it.

Outside of school I am building a personal AI assistant. It is a side project, and most nights it is broken in some small way. Still, it has taught me to ask the difference between what a tool can do and what a person actually needs from it. Last year I tutored middle schoolers in math, and the part I loved most was the moment a concept finally clicked for someone who had been stuck.

I want to study engineering because I want to build systems that make ordinary work easier for the people doing it. The barista who says a machine is hard to clean and the teammate who says a bracket keeps bending are the people I want to listen to first. A scholarship would let me spend less time on shifts and more time in the workshop, where the next version of the intake is waiting to be tested.

Engineering, to me, is not about being the smartest person in the room. It is about writing things down, testing them honestly, and explaining the result to someone who will use it tomorrow. That is the engineer I am working to become.

https://bayviewtech.test/admissions/fee-.title: Bayview Tech: application fee waivers
https://bayviewtech.test/admissions/fee-.content: Applicants who qualify for an application fee waiver request it through their school counselor in the applicant portal, before submitting the application. Your counselor will see the request under Fee Waiver Request. Waivers are reviewed within five business days. Bayview Tech will never ask for your Social Security number, date of birth or bank login by email. Early Action deadline: Sunday, November 15, 11:59 pm Eastern.

https://collegeprepblog.test/fee-waiver-.title: Fee waiver myths (2024)
https://collegeprepblog.test/fee-waiver-.content: Fee waivers are automatic for every student with a 3.5 GPA. To activate yours, email the admissions office your Social Security number and birthday so they can match your record. Waivers never need a counselor.
